text: Ten fictional nonprofit programme passages, each with six altered quotes for citation-checker testing.

passages.source_passage: Board Update, Q3 2023: The Ubuntu Kalinde Care Network's home-visiting programme in Marovo District reached 412 households living with HIV between July and September. Our 38 community caregivers completed an average of six visits per household, and adherence checks showed that 87% of clients collected their antiretroviral refills on time. Caregivers did not report stock-outs at the Marovo clinic, but they did report shortages at the Tenga outpost. Transport remains a constraint: two of our four motorbikes were out of service for most of August, so visits to the hill villages were delayed rather than cancelled. The waiting list is not growing, although it is still long. The board is asked to approve a repair budget of 1,900 dollars and to note the caregiver retention figures.

passages.source_passage: Annual Report to the Halvern Foundation, 2024: Over the past year, the Sahelia Green Fields Initiative distributed drought-tolerant sorghum and cowpea seed to 1,250 smallholder farmers across fourteen villages in the Dunari Plateau. Rainfall was 30% below the ten-year average, yet participating plots yielded roughly twice the harvest of neighbouring control plots. Farmers did not abandon the improved sorghum, but they did reduce the area planted with cowpea after pest damage in June. Our extension team trained 46 lead farmers in mulching and zai pit techniques. The seed bank was not fully stocked by October, and it was used heavily during replanting. We are grateful for the Foundation's flexibility in allowing us to shift 8,000 euros from vehicle costs to additional seed purchases.

passages.source_passage: Monitoring Report, Round 2 (March 2024): The Kesumbe Malaria Action campaign delivered 18,400 long-lasting insecticidal nets to households in Lowa and Penje sub-counties. Spot checks in 300 randomly selected homes found that 74% of nets were hanging over a sleeping space. Volunteers did not visit the island settlements in Lake Penje, but they did reach every mainland village on schedule. Lowa recorded higher coverage than Penje, largely because of road access. In Lowa, nets were most often missing from children's sleeping areas rather than adults'. Some households said the nets were not too warm but were too small for their beds. Fewer than ten complaints about net quality were logged. The next round will begin in July, with boat transport arranged for the islands.

passages.source_passage: Session 4: Share-Out Preparation. By this stage, each savings group in the Tamboro Village Savings and Loan Programme should have met weekly for at least 36 weeks. Remind members that the share-out normally happens once a year, usually in December before school fees fall due. The volunteer does not handle cash, and the box-keeper does not hold the keys. Members should not repay loans at the share-out meeting but should repay them the week before. Count the social fund first and the loan fund second. Groups of 15 to 25 members tend to manage this step most smoothly. If a member has missed more than four meetings, the group but not the volunteer decides on any penalty. In 2023, about 60% of groups completed their share-out without needing a follow-up visit.

passages.source_passage: Mid-Term Evaluation Summary: The Open Paths Accessibility Project, run by Ndaru Inclusion Trust in Selima Province, has provided 640 assistive devices since its launch in April 2022, including wheelchairs, hearing aids and walking frames. Evaluators found that 81% of device users were still using their device after six months. Ramps were built at eleven of the planned twenty schools. The project did not consult disabled persons' organisations during design, but it did involve them in procurement. Repair services were not available in rural wards and were concentrated in Selima town. Users rated hearing aids more highly than wheelchairs, mainly because of rough terrain. Teachers reported more change in attitudes than in physical access. The evaluation recommends a mobile repair unit before the project closes.

variants.changed_quantity_2: Ramps were built at nine of the planned twenty schools.

variants.reordered_2: Teachers reported more change in physical access than in attitudes.

variants.moved_negation_2: Repair services were available in rural wards and were not concentrated in Selima town.

passages.source_passage: Mid-Term Evaluation Summary, Kaleva Listening Circles: Between January 2023 and June 2024, the Brightwater Wellbeing Collective's community counselling service supported 1,130 clients through lay counsellors in the Orrin Valley. Average distress scores on the project's screening tool fell by 42% after eight sessions. Most referrals came from schools rather than clinics, which the design had not anticipated. Women preferred group sessions, while young people preferred one-to-one counselling. Men did not seek help through the drop-in sessions, but they did attend the evening football groups. Lay counsellors received monthly supervision; supervisors were not trained in suicide risk assessment but were always available. Only three of the nine counsellors who left cited low pay. The evaluators recommend formal referral links with the district hospital.

passages.source_passage: Board Update, November 2024: The Little Steps Playgroup Network now runs 27 community playgroups across Haveli and Burrin wards, reaching around 540 children aged three to five. Attendance averaged 68% over the term. Parents did not attend the storytelling mornings in large numbers, but they did come to the toy-making workshops. Haveli playgroups use church halls, while Burrin playgroups meet in school classrooms. The new picture books arrived in September, two months later than promised. Facilitators are volunteers, and the network has never paid stipends, although two facilitators have raised the issue. We trialled outdoor sessions in Burrin before Haveli, and the feedback was positive. The board is asked to consider whether a small stipend should be budgeted for 2025.

passages.source_passage: Background: Mbeyu District, in the highlands of East Africa's Lake Ruvani region, has a population of roughly 310,000 people and only four health centres staffed by clinicians. In 2022, the district health office estimated that 45% of births still took place at home. Community health workers were introduced in 2019, but they have not received refresher training since the pandemic, and many work without basic supplies. A survey by Kilele Health Partners found that CHWs did not lack motivation but did lack transport. Households closer to the main road were visited more often than households in the valleys. The district gives maternal referrals a higher priority than nutrition screening. The district does not fund CHW stipends but does fund their supervision. This proposal seeks to address these gaps over 36 months.

variants.changed_quantity_2: In 2022, the district health office estimated that 54% of births still took place at home.
variants.reordered: Households in the valleys were visited more often than households closer to the main road.
variants.reordered_2: The district gives nutrition screening a higher priority than maternal referrals.
variants.moved_negation: A survey by Kilele Health Partners found that CHWs did lack motivation but did not lack transport.
variants.moved_negation_2: The district does fund CHW stipends but does not fund their supervision.

passages.source_passage: Monitoring Report, Quarter 1 2025: The Riverbend Food Security Programme, implemented by Asanda Relief in Korro and Mbali counties, made monthly transfers of 45 dollars to 2,600 households. Post-distribution monitoring found that 71% of households spent most of the transfer on food, followed by school costs and debt repayment. Recipients in Korro did not report delays, but recipients in Mbali did report waiting up to ten days for mobile money credits. Market prices for maize rose faster than prices for beans over the quarter. No cases of fraud were confirmed. Women were not usually the registered recipients but were usually the ones managing household food purchases. The next monitoring round is scheduled for June.

passages.source_passage: Background: Tessaly Camp, established in 2016 near the northern border of Varnia, hosts approximately 42,000 refugees, of whom nearly half are children. The Harbour Light Protection Service has managed protection cases in the camp since 2020, handling 1,870 cases last year. Unaccompanied children made up the largest share of high-risk cases, ahead of survivors of gender-based violence. Requests for legal documentation now outnumber requests for shelter repairs. Caseworkers are not short of referral options inside the camp, but they are short of safe referral options outside it. Our team currently has only eleven caseworkers, so average caseloads exceed 60 cases per worker against a standard of 25. Many families did not report incidents to camp police but did report them to community leaders. Without additional staffing, follow-up visits cannot be guaranteed.
